questions.question: What is Angular, and how is an Angular application structured?
questions.title: Angular and Its Application Structure
questions.direct_answer: Angular is a web framework for building client applications from components. A component owns a part of the screen, its template describes that view, services hold reusable logic, dependency injection supplies dependencies, and the router can choose which component tree appears for a URL.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Angular builds an application as a tree of components.
A component joins a TypeScript class, an HTML template, and metadata.
Services hold shared logic or state that does not belong to one view.
Dependency injection creates and supplies services where they are needed.
The router maps browser URLs to component trees in larger applications.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Angular is a web framework for building client-side applications with TypeScript, HTML, and CSS. Its central idea is composition: the page is split into components, and those components form a tree. The root component is attached to the host page, and each child component owns a smaller piece of the interface.

A component class stores state and behavior. Its template declares what Angular should render, and the `@Component` metadata connects the class, selector, template, styles, and imported dependencies. Angular evaluates template bindings from component state and listens for user events. Reusable work that is not view-specific—such as loading products or storing a session—is usually placed in a service and supplied through dependency injection.

For example, a shop can have `AppComponent` at the root, a routed `ProductsPage` below it, and a reusable `ProductCard` for every item. The page asks `ProductService` for data, while each card receives one product as an input and emits a selection event.

Angular does not require every application to have the same folder tree, and modern Angular components are standalone by default. Older applications may organise features with `NgModule` classes, so a developer needs to recognise both styles. The useful mental model is not a list of files: it is a component tree for views, services for reusable work, dependency injection for construction, and optional routing for navigation.

sections.title: The component tree and shared application services
sections.content:
An Angular application begins with one root component. That component can render ordinary HTML and other components, which can render more children. This tree gives each part of the screen a clear owner. A product card should manage card behaviour; a products page should coordinate the list; the root should provide the application shell rather than contain every feature.

Templates are more than stored HTML strings. Angular compiles them and connects expressions such as `{{ title }}`, property bindings, event listeners, and control-flow blocks to the component. When a value used by a template changes and Angular is notified, Angular checks the relevant view and updates the affected DOM binding instead of rebuilding the whole document.

Services sit beside the visual tree. A service can fetch data, apply business rules, or share state. Dependency injection decides which service instance a component receives. Routing is another optional layer: it interprets the URL and places the matched component into a router outlet.

A small application may need only a root and a few child components. A larger one may add routes, lazy feature boundaries, and several provider scopes. These are design choices, not mandatory layers. The architecture stays understandable when every component has a focused view responsibility and shared logic is moved only when it is genuinely shared.

sections.title: Responsibilities in an Angular application
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Browser[Browser URL and events] --> Root[Root component]
  Root --> Page[Routed page component]
  Page --> Child[Reusable child components]
  Page --> DI[Dependency injection]
  DI --> Service[Shared service]
  Service --> Data[API or application state]
```

questions.question: What are standalone components, and how does Angular bootstrap an application?
questions.title: Standalone Components and Application Bootstrap
questions.direct_answer: A standalone component declares the template dependencies it uses in its own `imports` metadata instead of being declared by an `NgModule`. `bootstrapApplication` creates the application and renders a standalone root component, while application-wide providers can be passed in its configuration.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Modern Angular components are standalone by default.
A standalone component lists template dependencies in `imports`.
`bootstrapApplication` starts the app from a standalone root component.
Application-wide providers belong in bootstrap configuration or root provisioning.
Older `NgModule`-based applications remain valid and can be migrated gradually.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A standalone component is an Angular component that can be imported directly by another component, route, or bootstrap call. It does not need to be placed in an `NgModule.declarations` array. In current Angular, components are standalone by default; older code often writes `standalone: true` explicitly because that default changed in Angular 19.

The component's `imports` array names the directives, pipes, and child components available to its template. This makes a template's dependencies local and visible. At the application boundary, `bootstrapApplication(RootComponent, config)` creates the Angular application, instantiates the standalone root, and attaches it to the matching host element. The optional configuration supplies providers such as routing or HTTP support.

For example, a root component can import `WelcomeCard` and use `<welcome-card />` in its template. The main file passes the root to `bootstrapApplication` and can call `provideRouter(routes)` in the provider list.

Standalone does not mean that the component has no dependencies or that Angular creates a separate application for it. It changes how compilation dependencies are declared. `NgModule` remains important in existing libraries and applications, and Angular supports interoperability between the two models. For new code, standalone building blocks usually reduce indirection; for an existing module-based codebase, gradual migration is safer than rewriting working features only to change organisation.

sections.title: Compilation imports and runtime providers
sections.content:
Two lists that look similar solve different problems. A component's `imports` list tells Angular which template features can be compiled in that component. If the template uses another standalone component or a directive such as `NgClass`, that dependency belongs there. Missing it normally produces a template error.

Providers configure runtime dependency injection. An application provider created during `bootstrapApplication` is available through the application injector. Route or component providers can create narrower instances. Moving a service into a component's `imports` does not provide it, and putting a component in `providers` does not make its selector available to the template.

The browser first loads the JavaScript entry point. `bootstrapApplication` creates the application environment, resolves the configured providers, finds the root selector in the host document, and renders the root component. Child imports then allow the root template to create its declared children.

A standalone design still needs sensible feature boundaries. Direct imports can become noisy if every low-level item is pulled into every page, while shared import arrays can hide dependencies again. Keep dependencies near the component that uses them and use route-level lazy loading when a feature should load separately.

sections.title: Standalone bootstrap path
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Main[main.ts] --> Bootstrap[bootstrapApplication]
  Config[Application providers] --> Bootstrap
  Bootstrap --> Root[Standalone root component]
  RootImports[Root imports] --> Root
  Root --> Host[app-root host element]
  Root --> Children[Imported child components]
```

questions.question: How does Angular render and update a component tree when state changes?
questions.title: Rendering and Change Detection
questions.direct_answer: Angular creates views from compiled component templates, evaluates their bindings, and writes the results to the DOM. When Angular receives a change notification—such as a signal update, an event, a new input, or an explicit mark—it checks the relevant views and updates bindings whose values changed.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Angular compiles templates into instructions that create and update views.
A component tree gives Angular an ordered set of views to check.
Signals read by a template notify Angular when their values change.
Events and new bound inputs also schedule the relevant view for checking.
Angular updates changed bindings; it does not replace the whole page DOM.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Angular renders a component by running instructions produced from its compiled template. On the first pass, those instructions create DOM nodes and evaluate bindings. Child component selectors create child views, so the application becomes a view tree that follows the component tree.

Later, Angular needs a notification that state may have changed. Current Angular can receive that notification from a signal used in a template, a template or host event, a new input set by a parent, the `AsyncPipe`, or an explicit change-detection API. Angular then checks the relevant views, evaluates their bindings again, compares the results, and writes changed values to the DOM.

For example, a template can display `{{ count() }}` from a signal. Clicking a button calls `count.update`. The signal notifies Angular, the text binding is reevaluated, and only the displayed count needs a DOM update.

Change detection is not the same as repainting the entire browser page, and mutating an ordinary object does not automatically produce a notification. A parent that passes the same object reference to an OnPush child can leave that child unchanged until another valid notification occurs. Signals or immutable input updates make this boundary explicit. The practical model is: state changes, Angular is notified, affected views are checked, and changed bindings update the DOM.

sections.title: Creation, notification, checking, and DOM update
sections.content:
Rendering has a creation phase and an update phase. Creation builds elements, text nodes, listeners, and child component views from the compiled template. The update instructions read component values and place them into text, properties, classes, or styles. Angular remembers previous binding results so later checks can avoid unnecessary DOM writes.

A check does not happen because JavaScript memory changed in the abstract. Angular needs a recognised notification. Template events provide one. Updating a signal read by a template provides another. New component inputs, `AsyncPipe` emissions, and calls such as `markForCheck` also connect outside work to the rendering system. This matters in zoneless applications, where developers cannot depend on Zone.js noticing unrelated asynchronous activity.

Consider a counter component. The initial render creates a paragraph and button and writes zero into the paragraph. A click listener updates the signal. Angular checks the component, obtains one instead of zero, and changes that text node. The button is not recreated.

Checks can still become expensive when templates call slow functions or large trees receive broad notifications. Derived values should use clear state or computed signals, and templates should stay cheap. Direct DOM changes are another boundary: Angular may overwrite them on a later binding update, so application-visible state should normally drive the template instead.

sections.title: The Angular view update cycle
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  State[Component state changes] --> Notice[Angular notification]
  Notice --> Check[Relevant views checked]
  Check --> Evaluate[Bindings evaluated]
  Evaluate --> Compare[New and previous values compared]
  Compare -->|changed| DOM[Affected DOM binding updated]
  Compare -->|same| Keep[Existing DOM kept]
```
